question: Why do conservators keep some excavated bronzes in cases of deliberately dry air?
answer: To halt bronze disease. Chloride from the soil lies in pits as cuprous chloride; with moisture and oxygen it turns into a pale green powder and releases acid, which attacks fresh metal and makes more chloride. Below about 40% relative humidity the reaction stalls and the powder stops spreading.
move: When damage feeds itself, cut off the one ingredient it cannot do without.
ask: What one ingredient keeps a problem in my life going, and could I cut it off?
source: Scott, Copper and Bronze in Art, 2002
reference: David A. Scott, Copper and Bronze in Art: Corrosion, Colorants, Conservation, Getty Conservation Institute, 2002
